title: Harvest
hookLine: thank God for food and farmers
tomorrow: why do some parishes keep a book of names in November?

lines: A FIELD, A TRUCK, A STOVE.
cards: A plate of tacos takes a few minutes to eat. Behind it: a field somebody planted, a truck that drove through the night, a cook who stood at a hot stove. So who do you thank?
The old Catholic answer is all of them, and God first.
One grace Catholics say before meals goes like this: "Bless us, O Lord, and these thy gifts, which we are about to receive from thy bounty, through Christ our Lord. Amen."

teach.b: Two words in that grace carry the whole idea. Gifts: the food isn't owed to you. Bounty: it came from someone's open hand.

A psalm paints the same picture, in the Douay-Rheims Bible: "The eyes of all hope in thee, O Lord: and thou givest them meat in due season. Thou openest thy hand, and fillest with blessing every living creature."
Meat there simply means food. Israel had a harvest ritual too.

teach.h: THE FIRST BASKET, AND THE STORY.
teach.b: In Deuteronomy, a farmer brings the first basket of the year's crop to the priest. And before he hands it over, he has to say his family's story out loud: a wandering ancestor, slavery in Egypt, the rescue, the land.
Only then does he set the basket down and say he has brought the firstfruits of the land God gave him. Here's one to tell a friend tonight: in that ritual, thanks isn't just a feeling.
It comes with remembering out loud where you came from.
Catholic harvest thanks keeps both halves: God first, and the people whose hands are on the food.
That's why grace sits easily right next to thanking the cook, and why some parishes bless fields and gardens in their season.

how: Catholics say grace before meals, often the traditional 'Bless us, O Lord'; some parishes bless fields, gardens or harvest food, and Thanksgiving Day Masses give thanks for the harvest.

games.q: at a team cookout, the coach says 'dig in' and everyone grabs plates. you'd like to give thanks. what fits the harvest teaching best?
o: a quiet grace, then thank whoever cooked, out loud.
skip it; grace only counts if the whole table prays.
wait and say grace at home later, in private.
games.why: the grace thanks God for the gifts; harvest thanks also honors the hands behind them. both fit before the first bite.

practice: Take one small bite of something, a cracker, a piece of fruit, a sip of water, and before you swallow, slow all the way down.

Name, silently, three pairs of hands that touched it before you did: someone who grew it, someone who moved it, someone who made it. If you pray, the old grace is right there: bless us, O Lord, and these thy gifts.

wordCard.voice: Harvest. What the season grew, received as a gift, with thanks to God and to the hands behind it.

carryVoice: Pocket this one: the harvest. Gifts, from an open hand, carried to you by a lot of other hands.
